newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Oil market hangs on Iraq's export strategy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil market hangs on Iraq's export strategy.

text.p: The oil market braced for a surge in Iraqi crude oil exports after the last major obstacle to resuming the United Nations "oil-for-food" deal was removed on Monday, but traders said the impact on oil prices would depend on Baghdad's strategy in the weeks and months ahead.

The approval by the U.N. Secretary General of Baghdad's aid distribution plan means that Iraqi oil exports, after an absence of two months, should resume in a few days, assuming routine approval of export contracts and a pricing formula.
Analaysts and traders said that Iraq's strategy will dominate the oil market and likely will keep prices volatile.
"The absolute importance of the Iraqi export cannot be over-estimated," said Paul Ting, senior international oil analyst at Salomon Brothers.

"The immediate outlook for oil prices is decidedly bearish. However, oil prices may be facing another critical cross road during October...triggered by possible strategic shifts in Iraqi exports," Ting said, in a note to clients.
Indeed, the immediate question for the oil market is how much Iraq will try to export over the next month.

Because Iraq delayed restarting the second round of its deal with the U.N. for nearly two months, apparently to make a political point about delays in approving aid, it must sell around $1 billion of oil by September 5 or forego some of its allowance, according to U.N. officials.
(Under the terms of the deal, Iraq is allowed to export $2.14 billion of oil over 180 days in two equal instalments, with the period starting on June 8.)

Oil traders have received mixed messages from Baghdad about whether Baghdad intends to try to sell its full intitlement over the next month, which would mean selling around 1.6 million barrels per day (bpd).

One crude trader from a company which had a contract to lift Iraqi oil earlier this year, said the State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) in Baghdad gave assurances that it does not intend to flood the market once exports resume.
"They are not going to flood the market. We've been told they plan to pump at 700,000 to 800,000 barrels per day in an orderly fashion," said the trader.
However, other traders said they expected SOMO to try to reach $1 billion.
"I don't see any reason why they wouldn't export the entire amount," said the government crude contract negotiator for a major U.S. oil company with an Iraq contract during the first round.

"The feeling we get is that they'll want us to lift two VLCCs (Very Large Crude Carriers - about four million barrels) in the first 90 days if we want to renew our contract," said another oil company executive.

"We think Iraq will initially export around 1.5 to 1.6 million barrels per day, taking some out of storage at (the Turkish port of) Ceyhan and Mina (al Bakr in the Gulf)," said Roger Diwan, an analyst at Petroleum Finance Corp, a Washington consultancy.
He estimates that there is around 10 million barrels in storage at the two lifting centers, while Iraq has the ability to export around 1.3 million bpd on a regular basis.
Over the longer term, Ting of Salomon says he expects the run up to October 13 and the next review of the U.N. Special Commission on Iraqi disarmament (UNSCOM) likely will be a period of volatility.

He says Baghdad, having clearly signalled its displeasure with the current "oil-for-aid" regime, which it has always complained infringed on its sovereignty, will be making another big push for a full removal of the broader sanctions, which have been in place since 1990.
